courses.name: The Atlantic World, 1450-1800
courses.syllabus_body:
HIST 210 — The Atlantic World, 1450–1800

Professor Ada Whitfield · whitfield@example.edu · Fall 2026

Lecture: MWF 10:00-10:50 AM in Rice Hall 130

Discussion section: Thursdays 3:00–3:50 pm, Wilson Hall 214

Office hours: Wednesday 1:00-3:00 pm in Nau Hall 486, or by appointment.

Grading

ComponentWeight
Participation & section15%
Short response papers20%
Midterm examination25%
Research essay40%

Late Work

Written work loses 5% per day late, including weekends. After seven days work will not be accepted and receives a zero. You have two late passes for the term, each worth 48 hours, no questions asked; email me before the deadline to use one.

Attendance

Attendance in discussion section is required. More than 3 unexcused absences will lower your participation grade by one full letter. Lectures are not taken for attendance but the exams draw heavily on material that appears only in lecture.

Academic Integrity

All work must be your own. Plagiarism, including uncited paraphrase, is reported to the Honor Committee without exception. When in doubt, cite your sources.

Generative AI

You may use AI tools such as ChatGPT or Claude to brainstorm and to check your prose. You may not submit AI-generated text as your own writing, and any use must be disclosed in a short note at the end of the assignment. Undisclosed use is treated as plagiarism.

Required Texts

  • John Thornton, Africa and Africans in the Making of the Atlantic World, 2nd ed. ISBN 978-0521627245
  • Course reader, available from the Bookstore. ISBN 978-1234567897
  • Optional: Alison Games, The Web of Empire ISBN 978-0195335507

Schedule of Key Dates

  • Midterm examination: October 14, in class
  • No class November 25 – Thanksgiving recess
  • Research essay due December 8
  • Final exam: December 16, 9:00 am
courses.public_description: A survey of the making of the Atlantic world, from the first Portuguese voyages to the age of revolutions.

assignments.name: Response Paper 1: Thornton, chapters 1-3
assignments.description:
Write a 600-800 word response to Thornton, chapters 1-3.

  • Identify the central claim Thornton is making about African agency.
  • Explain what evidence he uses to support it.
  • Argue whether you find the evidence sufficient, and say why.

Submit as a PDF. Double-spaced, 12-pt Times New Roman. Chicago style footnotes.

assignments.name: Response Paper 2: The Middle Passage
assignments.description:
A 600-800 word response to this week's primary documents on the Middle Passage.

  • Choose one document from the reader and read it closely.
  • Describe what the document lets you see, and what it structurally cannot show.
  • Connect your reading to one argument from the Thornton chapters.

Submit as a PDF, double-spaced, with Chicago footnotes. At least 3 sources.

assignments.name: Midterm Examination
assignments.description: In-class midterm, 75 minutes. Covers weeks 1-7: lectures, the Thornton chapters, and all primary documents in the reader. Format: two short identifications and one essay. You must bring a blue book.

assignments.name: Research Essay

rubric.long_description: A specific, contestable claim sustained across the essay.

ratings.description: A clear, arguable thesis that the essay actually defends throughout
A thesis, but the essay drifts from it

rubric.long_description: Evidence drawn from the assigned primary documents, read critically.

ratings.description: Primary sources are read against the grain, not just quoted
Sources quoted accurately but taken at face value
Positions the argument against at least two secondary readings
Mentions secondary work without engaging it

assignments.description:
A 3000-4000 word research essay on a topic of your choosing within the scope of the course, approved by me in advance.

  • Submit a one-paragraph proposal and working bibliography by week 9.
  • Build an argument from at least 4 primary sources.
  • Engage at least 3 secondary works in the historiography.
  • Include a complete Chicago-style bibliography.
  • You must complete two peer reviews within one week of the deadline.

Submit as a PDF. Double-spaced, 12-pt font.

assignments.name: Section Participation
assignments.description: Assessed at the end of term based on your contribution to discussion section.

courses.name: Systems Programming
courses.syllabus_body:
CS 250: Systems Programming

Instructor: Dr. Marcus Oyelaran (oyelaran@example.edu). TA: Priya Raghavan.

Lecture meets TR 2:00-3:15 pm, Olsson 120. Lab: W 4:00-5:50 pm, Thornton A238.

Office hours Tuesdays 11:00 am - 12:30 pm, Rice 422.

Grading in this course is points-based. There are no category weights; your grade is your total points over the points available.

Late Policy

Each problem set may be submitted up to 48 hours late for a 20% penalty. Beyond 48 hours the autograder closes and no credit is available. There are no extensions on the final project.

Collaboration

You may discuss approaches with classmates. You may not share code. All submitted code is run through a similarity checker; matches are referred to the Honor Committee.

AI Tools

Use of Copilot, ChatGPT and similar tools is permitted on problem sets and forbidden on exams. You must be able to explain every line you submit.

Materials

  • Bryant & O'Hallaron, Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective, 3rd ed. ISBN 978-0134092669
  • A laptop that can run Linux in a VM or container
courses.public_description: How a program becomes a process: memory, linking, concurrency and the operating system interface.

assignments.name: Problem Set 3: Dynamic Memory
assignments.description:
Implement a memory allocator.

  • Implement malloc, free and realloc in mm.c.
  • Your allocator must achieve at least 70% utilisation on the trace suite.
  • Document your free-list design in a README.
  • Do not use any library allocator.

Submit as a .zip containing mm.c and README.

assignments.name: Lab 4: The Shell
assignments.description: Build a small shell supporting pipes and redirection. Complete the checkpoints in order; the lab TA signs off on each.

assignments.name: Final Project: A Concurrent Web Server

ratings.description: Handles 500 concurrent connections with no data races
Clear module boundaries, no global mutable state
Measured, reproducible, with the methodology stated

assignments.description:
In teams of three, build a concurrent web server in C.

  • Implement a thread pool with a bounded work queue.
  • Support HTTP/1.1 keep-alive.
  • Write a benchmark report of at least 1500 words comparing your server against a baseline.
  • Present a 10 minute demo in the last week of class.

Submit a repository URL and a PDF report.

assignments.name: Quiz 5
assignments.description: Twenty minutes, covering caching and the memory hierarchy. One attempt.

courses.name: Introductory Biology
courses.syllabus_body:
BIO 101 Introductory Biology. Dr. Helen Marsh, marsh@example.edu.

Your final grade is composed of the following: weekly quizzes are worth 20%, three unit exams are worth 45% total, the lab notebook is worth 20%, and the final exam is worth 15%.

Missed exams cannot be made up except with a documented medical excuse, submitted within 5 days of the missed exam.

Lab safety training must be completed before the first lab. Students without it are turned away.

assignments.name: Lab Notebook, Weeks 1-4
assignments.description: Scan and upload your lab notebook pages for weeks 1 through 4. Each entry must include the date, the aim, the procedure as performed, and your raw data.

assignments.name: Unit Exam 1
assignments.description: Covers cell structure, membranes and bioenergetics. Bring a pencil and your student ID.

assignments.name: Weekly Quiz 4
assignments.description: Ten questions on this week's reading. Two attempts, highest score counts.

announcements.title: Lab safety training due before Thursday
announcements.message: Please complete the online lab safety module before your first lab session. Students who have not completed it will not be admitted to the lab.
